newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland, Ukraine to face past in building future.
newsitem.headline: Poland, Ukraine to face past in building future.

text.p: Poland and Ukraine are set to sign a declaration next week laying to rest the ghosts of centuries of blood-soaked rivalry, an aide to President Aleksander Kwasniewski said on Thursday.

Kwasniewski and Ukraine's Leonid Kuchma are expected to agree details of a declaration on reconciliation during the Polish leader's three-day official visit to Ukraine from Tuesday, Marek Siwiec told a news conference.
"We don't ask for any forgiveness, but we just say what happened, what was bloody, that we want to condemn it," said Siwiec, head of the presidential National Security Office.

Poland was the first state to recognise Ukraine's independence in 1991 and it has put increasing emphasis on cultivating close ties with its large neighbour, a state also wanting to consolidate its new-found freedom from Moscow's dominance.
It has championed Kiev's efforts to bind itself to regional and Western international structures.
"We are accompanying Ukraine...in building its own sovereignty, strengthening its independence," Siwiec said.

Despite frequent cordial contacts at the top, relations are coloured by a history of religious and territorial rivalry and mutual blood-letting from 17th century cossack revolts against Polish rule until after World War Two.

The most delicate issues concern killings of Poles by the Ukrainian Insurrectionary Army (UPA) in the two countries' borderlands during and after the war and the repressive measures Polish and Soviet authorities used to crush these nationalists.
Polish historians say many tens of thousands of Poles were murdered by the UPA in Wolyn, Western Ukraine after 1943.
Polish troops deported more than 150,000 Ukrainians and other related minorities from its southeastern areas to the distant north and west to crush the irregulars in 1947.
Open discussion of these and other politically sensitive events has only become possible since the fall of communism.
"There are still witnesses of what happened even 50 years ago...because their pain was never publicly expressed, this pain is still strongly alive," Siwiec told reporters.
Kwasniewski's visit starts in Kiev where he will address parliament and hold talks with Kuchma.

On May 22 he goes to Odessa for talks with city officials and a conference on building transport and energy supply links between the south Ukrainian city and Poland's Baltic coast port Gdansk -- projects which Siwiec said would be supported in part by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.

"Creating new communications links, new sources of energy supply, new transit routes, is an element of gaining independence from those ties which were bound up with the country's former status in the Soviet Union," Siwiec said.
Kwasniewski aims to further promote growing bilateral trade which rose to well over $1 billion in 1996 with the balance in Poland's favour.
Kwasniewski finishes with a visit to Zhitomir, a town which was in Poland before the war and has a large Polish minority.
The visit will also deal with security issues. Unlike Russia, Ukraine has not firmly opposed Poland's goal of joining NATO but is anxious not to remain in a "grey zone" of security.
Siwiec said a bilateral committee would meet on May 19 to discuss Poland's bid to join NATO, and conventional weapons reduction talks in Vienna.
